# Packages

Install once in the console (not in this file), for example
`install.packages(c("ggplot2", "dplyr", "tidyr", "survival", "survminer",
"pheatmap", "cluster"))`.

```{r packages}
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(survival)
library(survminer)
library(pheatmap)
library(cluster)

theme_set(theme_bw(base_size = 11))

# Same colours for the PAM50 subtypes in every figure
subtype_cols <- c(LumA = "#1f4e9c", LumB = "#6fa8dc", Her2 = "#e377c2",
                  Basal = "#d62728", Normal = "#2ca02c")
# Same colours for mutation status in every figure
status_cols <- c("Wild-type" = "grey70", "Mutant" = "#d62728")
```

# Data preparation (Report: Overall Analysis Workflow)

## Load the three data sets

```{r load-data}
# Clinical file: the first 4 lines are cBioPortal metadata starting with '#'
clinical <- read.delim("dataset/data_clinical_patient.txt", skip = 4,
                       quote = "", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)

# Mutations: one row per mutation (MAF format), keep the columns we need
mutations <- read.delim("dataset/data_mutations.txt", quote = "",
                        stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
mutations <- mutations[, c("Hugo_Symbol", "Variant_Classification",
                           "Variant_Type", "Tumor_Sample_Barcode")]

# Expression: only the header is needed to know which patients have
# RNA-seq (the full matrix is analysed in Report 2)
rna_header  <- readLines("dataset/RNAseq_BRCA.csv", n = 1)
rna_samples <- gsub('"', "", strsplit(rna_header, ",")[[1]][-1])
# Keep tumour samples only (type code 01-09, while 10-19 are normal tissue)
rna_tumour <- rna_samples[as.numeric(substr(rna_samples, 14, 15)) < 10]

c(clinical_patients = nrow(clinical),
  mutation_rows     = nrow(mutations),
  rna_samples       = length(rna_samples),
  rna_tumour        = length(rna_tumour))
```

## Define the cohort: patients with clinical, mutation and expression data

TCGA barcodes use the first 12 characters (`TCGA-XX-XXXX`) for the patient.

```{r cohort}
mutations$PATIENT_ID <- substr(mutations$Tumor_Sample_Barcode, 1, 12)
rna_patients <- unique(substr(rna_tumour, 1, 12))
mut_patients <- unique(mutations$PATIENT_ID)

# Patients present in all three data sets
common <- Reduce(intersect, list(clinical$PATIENT_ID, mut_patients,
                                 rna_patients))
c(clinical = nrow(clinical), mutation = length(mut_patients),
  expression = length(rna_patients), all_three = length(common))
```

## Clean the clinical variables

```{r clean-clinical}
stage_raw <- clinical$AJCC_PATHOLOGIC_TUMOR_STAGE

cohort <- clinical %>%
  mutate(
    AGE = as.numeric(AGE),
    SUBTYPE = factor(sub("BRCA_", "", SUBTYPE),
                     levels = c("LumA", "LumB", "Her2", "Basal",
                                "Normal")),
    # Collapse sub-stages (IIA, IIB, ...) into I-IV, STAGE X becomes NA
    STAGE = case_when(grepl("^STAGE IV",  stage_raw) ~ "IV",
                      grepl("^STAGE III", stage_raw) ~ "III",
                      grepl("^STAGE II",  stage_raw) ~ "II",
                      grepl("^STAGE I",   stage_raw) ~ "I",
                      TRUE ~ NA_character_),
    STAGE_GROUP = factor(case_when(
      STAGE %in% c("I", "II")   ~ "Early (I-II)",
      STAGE %in% c("III", "IV") ~ "Late (III-IV)")),
    HISTOLOGY = case_when(ICD_O_3_HISTOLOGY == "8500/3" ~ "Ductal",
                          ICD_O_3_HISTOLOGY == "8520/3" ~ "Lobular",
                          TRUE ~ "Other/Mixed"),
    # "1:DECEASED" becomes 1 and "0:LIVING" becomes 0
    OS_EVENT   = suppressWarnings(as.numeric(substr(OS_STATUS, 1, 1))),
    OS_MONTHS  = as.numeric(OS_MONTHS),
    PFS_EVENT  = suppressWarnings(as.numeric(substr(PFS_STATUS, 1, 1))),
    PFS_MONTHS = as.numeric(PFS_MONTHS)
  ) %>%
  filter(PATIENT_ID %in% common)

table(cohort$SEX)
table(cohort$SUBTYPE, useNA = "ifany")
table(cohort$STAGE, useNA = "ifany")
```

## Filter to non-synonymous (protein-changing) mutations

Silent, intronic, UTR, flanking, RNA and Splice_Region variants do not change
the protein sequence, which is why we remove them.

```{r nonsyn}
nonsyn_classes <- c("Missense_Mutation", "Nonsense_Mutation",
                    "Frame_Shift_Del", "Frame_Shift_Ins",
                    "In_Frame_Del", "In_Frame_Ins", "Splice_Site",
                    "Nonstop_Mutation", "Translation_Start_Site")

mut    <- mutations %>% filter(PATIENT_ID %in% common)
mut_ns <- mut %>% filter(Variant_Classification %in% nonsyn_classes)

c(all_mutations = nrow(mut), non_synonymous = nrow(mut_ns))
```

## Build the binary mutation matrix and per-patient features

```{r mut-matrix}
# Patients x genes matrix, 1 = at least one non-synonymous mutation
pairs <- distinct(mut_ns, PATIENT_ID, Hugo_Symbol)
mut_matrix <- unclass(table(factor(pairs$PATIENT_ID, levels = common),
                            pairs$Hugo_Symbol))
dim(mut_matrix)

# Percentage of patients with a mutation in each gene
gene_freq <- data.frame(gene = colnames(mut_matrix),
                        n_patients = colSums(mut_matrix)) %>%
  mutate(pct = 100 * n_patients / length(common)) %>%
  arrange(desc(n_patients))
head(gene_freq, 10)

# Mutation burden per patient and status of the key driver genes
drivers <- c("TP53", "PIK3CA", "CDH1", "GATA3", "MAP3K1", "KMT2C", "PTEN")
burden  <- mut_ns %>% count(PATIENT_ID, name = "N_NONSYN")

cohort <- cohort %>%
  left_join(burden, by = "PATIENT_ID") %>%
  mutate(N_NONSYN = coalesce(N_NONSYN, 0L))
for (g in drivers) {
  is_mut <- mut_matrix[cohort$PATIENT_ID, g] == 1
  cohort[[g]] <- factor(ifelse(is_mut, "Mutant", "Wild-type"),
                        levels = c("Wild-type", "Mutant"))
}

# Save the cleaned objects so teammates can load them directly
dir.create("processed", showWarnings = FALSE)
saveRDS(list(cohort = cohort, mut_ns = mut_ns, mut_matrix = mut_matrix,
             gene_freq = gene_freq), "processed/report1_objects.rds")
```

# Investigation 1: Cohort demographics (Report: Results 1)

```{r inv1-age, fig.height=3.2}
summary(cohort$AGE)

# Boxplot of age with each patient shown as a point
ggplot(cohort, aes(x = "", y = AGE)) +
  geom_boxplot(fill = "grey85", width = 0.4) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.12, alpha = 0.25, size = 0.8) +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(title = "Age at diagnosis", x = NULL, y = "Age (years)")
```

From the plot, we can see that the age at diagnosis ranges from 26 to 90
years, with a median of 58 years and a mean of 58.31 years. The spread is
fairly symmetric, which means there is no strong skew toward younger or older
patients.

```{r inv1-age-subtype, fig.height=3.2}
# Median age per subtype, then a Kruskal-Wallis test
tapply(cohort$AGE, cohort$SUBTYPE, median)

ggplot(cohort, aes(x = AGE, y = SUBTYPE, fill = SUBTYPE)) +
  geom_boxplot(show.legend = FALSE) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = subtype_cols, na.value = "grey70") +
  labs(title = "Age at diagnosis by PAM50 subtype",
       x = "Age (years)", y = "Subtype")

kruskal.test(AGE ~ SUBTYPE, data = cohort)
```

Based on the output above, age differs between the PAM50 subtypes
(Kruskal-Wallis p = 0.007058). From the plot, we can see that Basal patients
(median 54 years) and Her2 patients (median 56.5 years) are diagnosed younger
than LumA patients (median 60 years).

```{r inv1-categorical, fig.height=3.2}
# Number of patients in each subtype and stage
ggplot(filter(cohort, !is.na(SUBTYPE)), aes(x = SUBTYPE, fill = SUBTYPE)) +
  geom_bar(show.legend = FALSE) +
  geom_text(stat = "count", aes(label = after_stat(count)), vjust = -0.3) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = subtype_cols) +
  labs(title = "PAM50 molecular subtype", x = "Subtype", y = "Patients")

ggplot(filter(cohort, !is.na(STAGE)), aes(x = STAGE)) +
  geom_bar(fill = "grey40") +
  geom_text(stat = "count", aes(label = after_stat(count)), vjust = -0.3) +
  labs(title = "AJCC pathologic stage", x = "Stage", y = "Patients")

table(cohort$RACE)
table(cohort$HISTOLOGY)
```

From the plots, we can see that LumA is by far the largest subtype (499
patients), followed by LumB (197) and Basal (171). Most tumours are stage II
(581 patients), while only 18 patients are stage IV, which means late-stage
disease is rare in this cohort. Most tumours are ductal (740) and 163 are
lobular.

```{r inv1-survival}
c(deaths = sum(cohort$OS_EVENT, na.rm = TRUE),
  progression_events = sum(cohort$PFS_EVENT, na.rm = TRUE),
  median_followup_months = median(cohort$OS_MONTHS, na.rm = TRUE))

# Kaplan-Meier curves of overall survival for each subtype
fit_sub <- survfit(Surv(OS_MONTHS, OS_EVENT) ~ SUBTYPE, data = cohort)
ggsurvplot(fit_sub, data = cohort, pval = TRUE,
           palette = unname(subtype_cols),
           legend.labs = levels(cohort$SUBTYPE), legend.title = "Subtype",
           title = "Overall survival by PAM50 subtype",
           xlab = "Months", ylab = "Survival probability",
           ggtheme = theme_bw())
```

Based on the output above, there are only 136 deaths and the median
follow-up is about 27 months, which means survival tests in this cohort have
limited power. From the plot, we can see that overall survival still differs
between subtypes (log-rank p = 0.024).

# Investigation 2: Mutation landscape (Report: Results 2)

```{r inv2-types, fig.height=3.8}
# Count every mutation type and mark the ones we keep
type_counts <- mut %>%
  count(Variant_Classification) %>%
  mutate(kept = ifelse(Variant_Classification %in% nonsyn_classes,
                       "Non-synonymous (kept)", "Removed"))

ggplot(type_counts,
       aes(x = reorder(Variant_Classification, n), y = n, fill = kept)) +
  geom_col() + coord_flip() +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Non-synonymous (kept)" = "#1f4e9c",
                               Removed = "grey70")) +
  labs(title = "Mutation types in the cohort", x = "Mutation type",
       y = "Number of mutations", fill = "Filter")
```

From the plot, we can see that missense mutations are by far the most common
type, followed by silent mutations. After removing the variants that do not
change the protein, we keep 85360 of the 130300 mutations.

```{r inv2-burden, fig.height=3.5}
summary(cohort$N_NONSYN)

# One bar per patient, sorted from most to fewest mutations
burden_plot <- cohort %>% arrange(desc(N_NONSYN)) %>%
  mutate(PATIENT_ID = factor(PATIENT_ID, levels = PATIENT_ID))

ggplot(burden_plot, aes(x = PATIENT_ID, y = N_NONSYN, fill = SUBTYPE)) +
  geom_col(width = 1) +
  scale_y_log10() +
  scale_fill_manual(values = subtype_cols, na.value = "grey70") +
  labs(title = "Non-synonymous mutations per patient",
       x = paste0("Patients (n = ", nrow(cohort), ")"),
       y = "Mutations (log10 scale)", fill = "Subtype") +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_blank(), axis.ticks.x = element_blank())
```

From the plot, we can see that most patients carry between 26 and 70
non-synonymous mutations (median 41). However, a few hypermutated tumours
carry far more (up to 5340), which is why we use a log scale and
rank-based tests for mutation burden.

```{r inv2-burden-subtype, fig.height=3.5}
# Median burden per subtype, then a Kruskal-Wallis test
tapply(cohort$N_NONSYN, cohort$SUBTYPE, median)

ggplot(cohort, aes(x = SUBTYPE, y = N_NONSYN + 1, fill = SUBTYPE)) +
  geom_boxplot(show.legend = FALSE) + scale_y_log10() +
  scale_fill_manual(values = subtype_cols, na.value = "grey70") +
  labs(title = "Mutation burden by subtype", x = "Subtype",
       y = "Non-synonymous mutations + 1 (log10)")

kruskal.test(N_NONSYN ~ SUBTYPE, data = cohort)
```

Based on the output above, mutation burden differs strongly between subtypes
(Kruskal-Wallis p < 2.2e-16). From the plot, we can see that Her2 (median 72)
and Basal (median 69) tumours carry more than twice as many mutations as LumA
tumours (median 30), which fits with these subtypes being more genomically
unstable.

```{r inv2-topgenes, fig.height=4.2}
# Top 20 genes by percentage of patients mutated
top20 <- head(gene_freq, 20)
ggplot(top20, aes(x = reorder(gene, pct), y = pct)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#1f4e9c") + coord_flip() +
  geom_text(aes(label = sprintf("%.2f%%", pct)), hjust = -0.1, size = 3) +
  expand_limits(y = max(top20$pct) * 1.15) +
  labs(title = "Top 20 most frequently mutated genes", x = "Gene",
       y = "Patients with a non-synonymous mutation (%)")
```

From the plot, we can see that PIK3CA (34.39%) and TP53 (34.29%) are the two
most frequently mutated genes, followed by TTN, CDH1, GATA3 and MUC16. TTN and
MUC16 are very long genes, which means they collect random mutations and are
not likely to be drivers.

# Investigation 3: Driver genes vs PAM50 subtype (Report: Results 3)

```{r inv3-freq, fig.height=4.5}
# Percentage of patients mutated for each driver gene within each subtype
driver_long <- cohort %>%
  filter(!is.na(SUBTYPE)) %>%
  select(PATIENT_ID, SUBTYPE, all_of(drivers)) %>%
  pivot_longer(all_of(drivers), names_to = "gene",
               values_to = "status") %>%
  group_by(gene, SUBTYPE) %>%
  summarise(pct = 100 * mean(status == "Mutant"), n = n(),
            .groups = "drop") %>%
  mutate(gene = factor(gene, levels = drivers))

ggplot(driver_long, aes(x = SUBTYPE, y = pct, fill = SUBTYPE)) +
  geom_col(show.legend = FALSE) +
  facet_wrap(~ gene, nrow = 2) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = subtype_cols) +
  labs(title = "Driver gene mutation frequency by PAM50 subtype",
       x = "Subtype", y = "Patients mutated (%)") +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))
```

From the plot, we can see that TP53 is mutated mostly in Basal and Her2
tumours, while PIK3CA, CDH1, GATA3 and MAP3K1 are mutated mostly in luminal
tumours. On the other hand, PTEN looks similar across all subtypes.

```{r inv3-tests}
# Fisher's exact test of mutation status vs subtype for each gene
# (Monte-Carlo p-value for the 5x2 table), then BH correction
sub_tests <- lapply(drivers, function(g) {
  tab <- table(cohort$SUBTYPE, cohort[[g]])
  p <- fisher.test(tab, simulate.p.value = TRUE, B = 1e5)$p.value
  data.frame(gene = g,
             pct_mutated = round(100 * mean(cohort[[g]] == "Mutant"), 2),
             p_value = p)
})
sub_tests <- bind_rows(sub_tests) %>%
  mutate(p_adj_BH = p.adjust(p_value, "BH"))
knitr::kable(sub_tests, digits = 5,
             caption = "Mutation status vs PAM50 subtype")
```

Based on the output above, TP53, PIK3CA, CDH1, GATA3 and MAP3K1 are all
associated with subtype after correction (adjusted p = 0.00001, the smallest
value possible with 100000 simulations). KMT2C is borderline (adjusted
p = 0.06088) and PTEN is not associated with subtype (adjusted p = 0.97358).

```{r inv3-cooccurrence}
# Do TP53 and PIK3CA mutations occur in the same patients?
tab_tp53_pik3ca <- table(TP53 = cohort$TP53, PIK3CA = cohort$PIK3CA)
tab_tp53_pik3ca
fisher.test(tab_tp53_pik3ca)   # odds ratio < 1 means mutually exclusive
```

Based on the output above, only 80 patients carry both TP53 and PIK3CA
mutations, and the odds ratio is 0.45 (p = 4.494e-08). This means the two
genes tend to be mutually exclusive, which is likely because TP53 marks the
Basal and Her2 subtypes while PIK3CA marks the luminal subtypes.

# Investigation 4: Mutations vs other clinical variables (Report: Results 4)

## CDH1 mutation vs tumour histology (ductal vs lobular)

```{r inv4-cdh1, fig.height=3.2}
# 2x2 table of histology vs CDH1 status and Fisher's exact test
hist_df  <- cohort %>% filter(HISTOLOGY %in% c("Ductal", "Lobular"))
tab_cdh1 <- table(Histology = hist_df$HISTOLOGY, CDH1 = hist_df$CDH1)
tab_cdh1
round(100 * prop.table(tab_cdh1, 1), 2)
fisher.test(tab_cdh1)

ggplot(hist_df, aes(x = HISTOLOGY, fill = CDH1)) +
  geom_bar(position = "fill") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = status_cols) +
  labs(title = "CDH1 mutation status by histology", x = "Histology",
       y = "Patients", fill = "CDH1 status")
```

Based on the output above, CDH1 is mutated in 60.74% of lobular tumours but
only 2.70% of ductal tumours (odds ratio 55.11, p < 2.2e-16). CDH1 encodes
E-cadherin, and its loss is the hallmark of lobular carcinoma, which is why
this is the clearest association in our data.

## TP53 mutation vs age at diagnosis

```{r inv4-tp53-age, fig.height=3.2}
# Median age in each group, then a Wilcoxon rank-sum test
tapply(cohort$AGE, cohort$TP53, median)

ggplot(cohort, aes(x = TP53, y = AGE, fill = TP53)) +
  geom_boxplot(show.legend = FALSE) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = status_cols) +
  labs(title = "Age at diagnosis by TP53 status", x = "TP53 status",
       y = "Age (years)")

wilcox.test(AGE ~ TP53, data = cohort)
```

```{r inv4-tp53-age-values, include=FALSE}
age_med <- tapply(cohort$AGE, cohort$TP53, median)
```

Based on the output above, TP53-mutant patients are younger at diagnosis
(median `r age_med[["Mutant"]]` years) than wild-type patients (median
`r age_med[["Wild-type"]]` years), and the difference is significant
(Wilcoxon p = 0.007354). This fits with TP53 being common in the Basal
subtype, which tends to affect younger patients.

## Mutation burden vs age and stage

```{r inv4-burden, fig.height=3.2}
# Spearman correlation between age and mutation burden
cor.test(cohort$AGE, cohort$N_NONSYN, method = "spearman", exact = FALSE)

ggplot(cohort, aes(x = AGE, y = N_NONSYN + 1)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.35) +
  geom_smooth(method = "loess", colour = "#d62728") +
  scale_y_log10() +
  labs(title = "Mutation burden vs age", x = "Age (years)",
       y = "Non-synonymous mutations + 1 (log10)")
```

Based on the output above, mutation burden increases only slightly with age
(Spearman rho = 0.098, p = 0.001855). From the plot, we can see that the
trend line is almost flat, which means age explains very little of the
variation in burden.

```{r inv4-burden-stage, fig.height=3.2}
# Burden across stages, compared with a Kruskal-Wallis test
ggplot(filter(cohort, !is.na(STAGE)), aes(x = STAGE, y = N_NONSYN + 1)) +
  geom_boxplot(fill = "grey85") + scale_y_log10() +
  labs(title = "Mutation burden by stage", x = "Stage",
       y = "Non-synonymous mutations + 1 (log10)")

kruskal.test(N_NONSYN ~ STAGE, data = cohort)
```

From the plot, we can see that the boxes overlap across all stages, and the
test confirms there is no significant difference (Kruskal-Wallis p = 0.1457).
This means a higher mutation burden does not go with a more advanced stage in
this cohort.

# Investigation 5: Survival by mutation status (Report: Results 5)

```{r inv5-km-function}
# Helper that draws a Kaplan-Meier plot with a log-rank p-value
km_plot <- function(var, name, time = "OS_MONTHS", event = "OS_EVENT",
                    label = "Overall survival") {
  df  <- cohort[!is.na(cohort[[time]]) & !is.na(cohort[[event]]), ]
  f   <- as.formula(paste0("Surv(", time, ", ", event, ") ~ ", var))
  fit <- surv_fit(f, data = df)
  pal <- c("grey40", "#d62728", "#1f4e9c", "#e377c2", "#2ca02c",
           "#ff7f0e")
  ggsurvplot(fit, data = df, pval = TRUE, conf.int = FALSE,
             palette = pal[seq_along(fit$strata)],
             legend.title = name,
             legend.labs = sub(".*=", "", names(fit$strata)),
             title = paste(label, "by", name), xlab = "Months",
             ylab = "Survival probability", ggtheme = theme_bw())
}
```

```{r inv5-km-tp53, fig.height=4}
# Overall survival, TP53 mutant vs wild-type
km_plot("TP53", "TP53 status")
```

From the plot, we can see that the TP53 curves overlap, and the difference
is not significant (log-rank p = 0.4).

```{r inv5-km-pik3ca, fig.height=4}
# Overall survival, PIK3CA mutant vs wild-type
km_plot("PIK3CA", "PIK3CA status")
```

From the plot, we can see that PIK3CA status also does not separate overall
survival (log-rank p = 0.44).

```{r inv5-km-pfs, fig.height=4}
# Progression-free survival has a different event definition
km_plot("TP53", "TP53 status", "PFS_MONTHS", "PFS_EVENT",
        "Progression-free survival")
```

Since overall survival has few events, we also tried progression-free
survival. However, TP53 status is still not significant (log-rank p = 0.52).

```{r inv5-combined, fig.height=4}
# Four groups based on TP53 and PIK3CA together
cohort <- cohort %>%
  mutate(TP53_PIK3CA = factor(case_when(
    TP53 == "Mutant" & PIK3CA == "Mutant" ~ "Both",
    TP53 == "Mutant"                      ~ "TP53 only",
    PIK3CA == "Mutant"                    ~ "PIK3CA only",
    TRUE                                  ~ "Neither"),
    levels = c("Neither", "TP53 only", "PIK3CA only", "Both")))
table(cohort$TP53_PIK3CA)
km_plot("TP53_PIK3CA", "TP53 and PIK3CA status")
```

From the plot, we can see that the four groups (Neither 395, TP53 only 265,
PIK3CA only 266, Both 80) do not differ in overall survival (log-rank
p = 0.49).

```{r inv5-cox}
# Cox model to adjust mutation status for age and stage
cox <- coxph(Surv(OS_MONTHS, OS_EVENT) ~ TP53 + PIK3CA + AGE +
               STAGE_GROUP, data = cohort)
cox_tab <- cbind(summary(cox)$conf.int[, c(1, 3, 4)],
                 p = summary(cox)$coefficients[, 5])
colnames(cox_tab) <- c("HR", "CI_low", "CI_high", "p")
knitr::kable(cox_tab, digits = 3,
             caption = "Cox proportional hazards model (overall survival)")
cox.zph(cox)   # check of the proportional hazards assumption
```

Based on the output above, TP53 mutation becomes a significant risk factor
once we adjust for age and stage (HR = 1.617, 95% CI 1.120 to 2.334,
p = 0.010). This differs from the Kaplan-Meier result because TP53-mutant
patients are younger, and each extra year of age raises the risk of death
(HR = 1.039 per year), which hides the TP53 effect when age is ignored. Late stage has
the largest effect (HR = 3.077). However, `cox.zph()` shows that stage breaks
the proportional hazards assumption (p = 0.006), so this model should be
interpreted with care.

# Investigation 6: Clustering of the mutation matrix (Report: Results 6)

## Feature selection

```{r inv6-features}
# Use the 30 most frequently mutated genes as features
feat_genes <- head(gene_freq$gene, 30)
X <- mut_matrix[, feat_genes]

# Patients with no mutation in any feature gene have no defined binary
# distance, so we keep them aside as a "No frequent mutation" group
has_mut <- rowSums(X) > 0
table(has_mut)
Xc <- X[has_mut, ]

# Binary (Jaccard) distance between patients
d <- dist(Xc, method = "binary")
```

## Approach A: hierarchical clustering and Approach B: PAM (k-medoids)

```{r inv6-choose-k, fig.height=3}
# Approach A uses Ward.D2 linkage on the binary distance
hc <- hclust(d, method = "ward.D2")

# Average silhouette width for k = 2 to 8 with both methods
ks <- 2:8
sil <- data.frame(
  k = ks,
  Hierarchical = sapply(ks, function(k)
    mean(silhouette(cutree(hc, k), d)[, 3])),
  PAM = sapply(ks, function(k)
    pam(d, k, diss = TRUE)$silinfo$avg.width))
knitr::kable(sil, digits = 3, caption = "Average silhouette width")

sil %>%
  pivot_longer(-k, names_to = "method", values_to = "silhouette") %>%
  ggplot(aes(k, silhouette, colour = method)) +
  geom_line() + geom_point() +
  labs(title = "Choosing the number of clusters",
       x = "Number of clusters (k)", y = "Average silhouette width",
       colour = "Method")
```

Based on the output above, all silhouette widths are below 0.2, which means
the clusters are weak. This is expected because the mutation matrix is very
sparse. We use k = 4 because it gives clusters that are easy to interpret,
even though hierarchical clustering scores slightly higher at k = 3.

```{r inv6-cluster}
k <- 4   # chosen for interpretability (see the silhouette table)
cl_hc  <- cutree(hc, k)
cl_pam <- pam(d, k, diss = TRUE)$clustering

# Agreement between the two methods
table(Hierarchical = cl_hc, PAM = cl_pam)

# Add the hierarchical clusters to the cohort table
cohort$CLUSTER <- "No frequent mutation"
cohort$CLUSTER[match(rownames(Xc), cohort$PATIENT_ID)] <- paste0("C", cl_hc)
cohort$CLUSTER <- factor(cohort$CLUSTER,
                         levels = c(paste0("C", 1:k),
                                    "No frequent mutation"))
table(cohort$CLUSTER)
```

Based on the output above, almost all of hierarchical C1 (75 of 77 patients)
falls in PAM cluster 1, and all of C4 (54 patients) falls in PAM cluster 2.
However, PAM spreads the large mixed cluster C2 across all four of its
clusters, which shows that this group has no stable structure. We use the
hierarchical clusters for the rest of the analysis.

```{r inv6-heatmap, fig.height=7, fig.width=9.5, out.width="100%"}
# Heatmap of the feature genes, patients ordered by the dendrogram
ann <- data.frame(
  Subtype = cohort$SUBTYPE[match(rownames(Xc), cohort$PATIENT_ID)],
  Cluster = factor(paste0("C", cl_hc)),
  row.names = rownames(Xc))
pheatmap(t(Xc), cluster_cols = hc, cluster_rows = FALSE,
         color = c("white", "black"), legend = FALSE,
         annotation_col = ann,
         annotation_colors = list(Subtype = subtype_cols),
         show_colnames = FALSE, fontsize = 8, fontsize_row = 7,
         cutree_cols = k, treeheight_col = 30,
         main = paste("Top 30 mutated genes with patients clustered",
                      "(binary distance, Ward.D2)"))
```

From the heatmap, we can see that each small cluster is built around one or
two genes, such as GATA3 or TP53, while most patients fall into one large
mixed cluster.

## What characterises each cluster?

```{r inv6-profile}
# Percentage of patients mutated in each gene, per cluster
profile <- sapply(split(as.data.frame(Xc), cl_hc),
                  function(m) round(100 * colMeans(m), 1))
colnames(profile) <- paste0("C", colnames(profile))
top_rows <- order(-apply(profile, 1, max))
knitr::kable(head(profile[top_rows, ], 12),
             caption = "% of patients mutated in each gene, by cluster")
```

Based on the output above, C1 is a GATA3 cluster (98.7% mutated), C3 is a
PIK3CA cluster that also carries CDH1 and MAP3K1 mutations (74.1%, 36.8% and
24.1%), and C4 is a TP53-only cluster (100% TP53). C2 is a mixed cluster with
both TP53 (44.7%) and PIK3CA (35.1%) mutations.

## Clusters vs clinical data

```{r inv6-clinical, fig.height=3.5}
# Cluster vs subtype, with a simulated chi-square p-value
tab_cl <- table(cohort$CLUSTER, cohort$SUBTYPE)
tab_cl
chisq.test(tab_cl, simulate.p.value = TRUE, B = 1e5)

ggplot(filter(cohort, !is.na(SUBTYPE)), aes(x = CLUSTER, fill = SUBTYPE)) +
  geom_bar(position = "fill") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = subtype_cols) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  labs(title = "PAM50 subtype composition of each mutation cluster",
       x = "Cluster", y = "Patients", fill = "Subtype") +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 20, hjust = 1))

# Cluster vs early or late stage
chisq.test(table(cohort$CLUSTER, cohort$STAGE_GROUP))
```

From the plot, we can see that the clusters match the PAM50 subtypes closely
(p = 1e-05). C3 is almost all LumA (147 patients), and C4 is mostly Basal
(34 of the 54 patients). On the other hand, the clusters are not related to
stage (p = 0.5429).

```{r inv6-survival, fig.height=4}
# Overall survival for each mutation cluster
km_plot("CLUSTER", "Cluster")
```

From the plot, we can see that the clusters do not differ in overall survival
(log-rank p = 0.9). Overall, mutation clusters capture the subtype biology
but do not add prognostic information on their own.

# Investigation 7: Survival by race (Report: Results 7)

Question: does overall survival differ between racial groups, and if it does,
is the difference explained by subtype, stage or age, or by differences in
driver mutations?

## Define the race groups

`RACE` is self-reported. We keep the three groups with enough patients to
analyse (White, Black or African American, Asian). One American Indian or
Alaska Native patient and the patients with no race recorded are removed,
because a single patient or an unknown group cannot be compared.

```{r inv7-race-groups}
race_cols <- c(White = "grey40", Black = "#d62728", Asian = "#1f4e9c")

race_df <- cohort %>%
  mutate(RACE3 = case_when(
    RACE == "White"                     ~ "White",
    RACE == "Black or African American" ~ "Black",
    RACE == "Asian"                     ~ "Asian")) %>%
  filter(!is.na(RACE3)) %>%
  mutate(RACE3 = factor(RACE3, levels = c("White", "Black", "Asian")),
         # Disease-specific survival: "1:DEAD WITH TUMOR" counts as an event
         DSS_EVENT  = suppressWarnings(as.numeric(substr(DSS_STATUS, 1, 1))),
         DSS_MONTHS = as.numeric(DSS_MONTHS))

c(kept = nrow(race_df), removed = nrow(cohort) - nrow(race_df))
```

## Who is in each group?

```{r inv7-race-summary}
race_summary <- race_df %>%
  group_by(Race = RACE3) %>%
  summarise(Patients        = n(),
            Median_age      = median(AGE, na.rm = TRUE),
            Deaths          = sum(OS_EVENT, na.rm = TRUE),
            Pct_died        = round(100 * Deaths / Patients, 1),
            Median_followup = round(median(OS_MONTHS, na.rm = TRUE), 1),
            # Deaths per 100 person-years corrects for unequal follow-up
            Deaths_per_100py = round(100 * Deaths /
                                     (sum(OS_MONTHS, na.rm = TRUE) / 12), 2))
knitr::kable(race_summary, caption = "Patients, deaths and follow-up by race")

kruskal.test(AGE ~ RACE3, data = race_df)
```

Based on the output above, we keep 918 patients (697 White, 162 Black, 59
Asian). Black and Asian patients are diagnosed younger (median 54 years) than
White patients (median 59 years; Kruskal-Wallis p = 0.005). The Asian group
has only 3 deaths and a short median follow-up (12.7 months), so any survival
estimate for this group is very uncertain. The death rate per 100
person-years is similar for White (3.93) and Black (4.12) patients.

## Subtype and stage mix by race

If one group has more aggressive subtypes (Basal, Her2), it may have worse
survival for that reason alone, so we check this before comparing survival.

```{r inv7-race-subtype, fig.height=3.6}
sub_df <- filter(race_df, !is.na(SUBTYPE))

ggplot(sub_df, aes(x = RACE3, fill = SUBTYPE)) +
  geom_bar(position = "fill") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = subtype_cols) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  scale_x_discrete(labels = function(x)
    paste0(x, "\n(n = ", table(sub_df$RACE3)[x], ")")) +
  labs(title = "PAM50 subtype mix by race", x = "Race",
       y = "Patients", fill = "Subtype")

tab_sub <- table(sub_df$RACE3, sub_df$SUBTYPE)
round(100 * prop.table(tab_sub, 1), 1)
chisq.test(tab_sub, simulate.p.value = TRUE, B = 1e5)
```

Based on the output above, the subtype mix differs strongly by race
(p = 1e-05, the smallest value possible with 100000 simulations). Basal
tumours make up 33.3% of tumours in Black patients, about twice the share in
White patients (15.6%). Asian patients have more Her2 (25.4%) and LumB
(27.1%) tumours. White patients have the most LumA tumours (56.6%), the
subtype with the best prognosis. The higher share of Basal tumours in Black
women matches previous population studies.

```{r inv7-race-stage}
tab_stage <- table(race_df$RACE3, race_df$STAGE_GROUP)
round(100 * prop.table(tab_stage, 1), 1)
fisher.test(tab_stage)
```

The share of late-stage (III-IV) tumours is similar across the three groups
(20-24%, Fisher p = 0.63), so stage at diagnosis does not differ by race in
this cohort.

## Overall and disease-specific survival by race

The Kaplan-Meier plots are cut at 120 months because very few patients are
followed beyond that, so the tail of the curves is unreliable. The log-rank
p-value uses all of the follow-up.

```{r inv7-km-os, fig.height=5.5}
fit_race_os <- survfit(Surv(OS_MONTHS, OS_EVENT) ~ RACE3, data = race_df)
ggsurvplot(fit_race_os, data = race_df, pval = TRUE, risk.table = TRUE,
           palette = unname(race_cols), legend.title = "Race",
           legend.labs = levels(race_df$RACE3),
           xlim = c(0, 120), break.time.by = 24,
           title = "Overall survival by race",
           xlab = "Months", ylab = "Survival probability",
           risk.table.height = 0.25, ggtheme = theme_bw())
survdiff(Surv(OS_MONTHS, OS_EVENT) ~ RACE3, data = race_df)
```

From the plot, we can see that the three curves overlap, and the log-rank
test finds no difference in overall survival (p = 0.89). The `survdiff`
output shows that each group has almost exactly the number of deaths
expected if all groups had the same risk (White 102 observed vs 102.7
expected, Black 24 vs 22.6, Asian 3 vs 3.7).

Overall survival counts deaths from any cause. Disease-specific survival only
counts patients who died with tumour, which removes deaths unrelated to the
cancer.

```{r inv7-km-dss, fig.height=5.5}
dss_df  <- filter(race_df, !is.na(DSS_EVENT), !is.na(DSS_MONTHS))
fit_race_dss <- survfit(Surv(DSS_MONTHS, DSS_EVENT) ~ RACE3, data = dss_df)
ggsurvplot(fit_race_dss, data = dss_df, pval = TRUE, risk.table = TRUE,
           palette = unname(race_cols), legend.title = "Race",
           legend.labs = levels(dss_df$RACE3),
           xlim = c(0, 120), break.time.by = 24,
           title = "Disease-specific survival by race",
           xlab = "Months", ylab = "Survival probability",
           risk.table.height = 0.25, ggtheme = theme_bw())
```

Disease-specific survival does not differ by race either (log-rank p = 0.82),
so the null result is not caused by deaths from other causes.

## Cox models: is the race effect explained by other variables?

We fit the same model three times, adding the possible confounders step by
step, and watch how the hazard ratio (HR) for each race changes. White
patients are the reference group (HR = 1).

```{r inv7-cox}
cox_df <- race_df %>% filter(!is.na(SUBTYPE), !is.na(STAGE_GROUP))

m1 <- coxph(Surv(OS_MONTHS, OS_EVENT) ~ RACE3, data = cox_df)
m2 <- coxph(Surv(OS_MONTHS, OS_EVENT) ~ RACE3 + AGE + STAGE_GROUP,
            data = cox_df)
m3 <- coxph(Surv(OS_MONTHS, OS_EVENT) ~ RACE3 + AGE + STAGE_GROUP + SUBTYPE,
            data = cox_df)

# Pull the race rows out of each model into one table
race_rows <- function(model, label) {
  s  <- summary(model)
  rr <- grep("^RACE3", rownames(s$coefficients))
  data.frame(Model = label,
             Term  = sub("RACE3", "", rownames(s$coefficients)[rr]),
             HR    = s$conf.int[rr, 1],
             CI_low  = s$conf.int[rr, 3],
             CI_high = s$conf.int[rr, 4],
             p     = s$coefficients[rr, 5])
}
cox_race <- bind_rows(race_rows(m1, "1. Race only"),
                      race_rows(m2, "2. + age, stage"),
                      race_rows(m3, "3. + age, stage, subtype"))
knitr::kable(cox_race, digits = 3, row.names = FALSE,
             caption = paste0("Hazard ratio for death vs White patients (n = ",
                              nrow(cox_df), ", ", sum(cox_df$OS_EVENT),
                              " deaths)"))
```

```{r inv7-cox-forest, fig.height=3.2}
ggplot(cox_race, aes(x = HR, y = Model, colour = Term)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 1, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_pointrange(aes(xmin = CI_low, xmax = CI_high),
                  position = position_dodge(width = 0.5)) +
  scale_x_log10() +
  scale_colour_manual(values = race_cols[c("Black", "Asian")]) +
  scale_y_discrete(limits = rev) +
  labs(title = "Hazard ratio for death vs White patients",
       x = "Hazard ratio (log scale, 95% CI)", y = NULL, colour = "Race")
```

```{r inv7-cox-full}
# Full adjusted model and the proportional hazards check
knitr::kable(cbind(HR = summary(m3)$conf.int[, 1],
                   CI_low = summary(m3)$conf.int[, 3],
                   CI_high = summary(m3)$conf.int[, 4],
                   p = summary(m3)$coefficients[, 5]),
             digits = 3, caption = "Fully adjusted Cox model (model 3)")
cox.zph(m3)
```

Based on the output above, race is not associated with survival in any of
the three models. The hazard ratio for Black vs White patients stays close to
1 (1.01 unadjusted, 1.11 after age and stage, 0.91 after also adding
subtype; all p > 0.67), and every confidence interval crosses 1. The Asian
intervals are very wide (about 0.4 to 4) because this group has only 3
deaths. Adding subtype moves the Black hazard ratio down slightly, which fits
with Basal tumours being more common in Black patients. In the full model,
age (HR = 1.04 per year), late stage (HR = 3.05) and the Her2 subtype
(HR = 2.50 vs LumA) are the significant predictors. As in Investigation 5,
stage breaks the proportional hazards assumption (`cox.zph` p = 0.009), so
its hazard ratio should be read with care.

## Driver mutations by race

To link race to the mutation data, we compare how often the main driver
genes are mutated in each group (Fisher's exact test per gene, then
Benjamini-Hochberg correction for testing several genes).

```{r inv7-race-drivers, fig.height=3.6}
drv_long <- race_df %>%
  select(RACE3, all_of(drivers)) %>%
  pivot_longer(all_of(drivers), names_to = "gene", values_to = "status") %>%
  group_by(gene, RACE3) %>%
  summarise(pct = 100 * mean(status == "Mutant"), .groups = "drop") %>%
  mutate(gene = factor(gene, levels = drivers))

ggplot(drv_long, aes(x = gene, y = pct, fill = RACE3)) +
  geom_col(position = "dodge") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = race_cols) +
  labs(title = "Driver gene mutation frequency by race", x = "Gene",
       y = "Patients mutated (%)", fill = "Race")

drv_tests <- bind_rows(lapply(drivers, function(g) {
  tab <- table(race_df$RACE3, race_df[[g]])
  data.frame(gene = g,
             White = round(100 * prop.table(tab, 1)["White", "Mutant"], 1),
             Black = round(100 * prop.table(tab, 1)["Black", "Mutant"], 1),
             Asian = round(100 * prop.table(tab, 1)["Asian", "Mutant"], 1),
             p = fisher.test(tab, simulate.p.value = TRUE, B = 1e5)$p.value)
})) %>% mutate(p_adj_BH = p.adjust(p, "BH"))
knitr::kable(drv_tests, digits = 4,
             caption = "% of patients mutated, by race (Fisher test, BH-adjusted)")
```

```{r inv7-tp53-nonbasal}
# TP53 is common in Basal tumours, so check whether any TP53 difference
# by race remains among non-Basal patients
nb <- filter(race_df, !is.na(SUBTYPE), SUBTYPE != "Basal")
tab_nb <- table(nb$RACE3, nb$TP53)
round(100 * prop.table(tab_nb, 1), 1)
fisher.test(tab_nb)
```

Based on the output above, three driver genes differ by race after BH
correction:

- **TP53** is mutated more often in Black (46.3%) and Asian (49.2%) patients
  than in White patients (30.8%; adjusted p = 0.0006).
- **PIK3CA** is mutated less often in Black patients (21.6%) than in White
  (36.6%) or Asian (40.7%) patients (adjusted p = 0.002).
- **CDH1** is mutated less often in Black patients (5.6% vs 13.9% in White;
  adjusted p = 0.019).

These differences mostly follow the subtype mix: TP53 marks Basal tumours,
which are more common in Black patients, while PIK3CA and CDH1 are luminal
genes. However, TP53 still differs by race among non-Basal patients (White
21.0%, Black 25.5%, Asian 42.3%; Fisher p = 0.003). This is driven by the
Asian group, which has many Her2 tumours (a TP53-rich subtype), so subtype
may still explain part of it.

## Summary and limitations

- Survival does not differ by race in this cohort, before or after adjusting
  for age, stage and subtype (log-rank p = 0.89; adjusted HR for Black vs
  White = 0.91, 95% CI 0.55-1.50).
- The tumours themselves differ: Black patients have twice the share of Basal
  tumours and more TP53 mutations, and Asian patients have more Her2 tumours.
- Limitations: race is self-reported and also reflects social and
  access-to-care factors, not only biology. The Black (24 deaths) and
  especially Asian (3 deaths) groups are small, and follow-up is short
  (median 25 and 13 months), so the study has low power to detect a real
  survival difference. TCGA patients were treated at academic centres, which
  may reduce differences in care seen in the general population.
